{{Nihongo|'''Hirotaka Sugawara'''|菅原 寛孝|Sugawara Hirotaka|born March 15, 1938}} is a Japanese physicist, specializing in the theoretical study of [[particle physics]].  He is known for the "Lee-Sugawara relation" and "A Field Theory of Currents"<ref name="field theory of currents">{{cite journal|last1=Sugawara|first1=Hirotaka|title=A Field Theory of Currents|journal=Physical Review|date=1968|volume=170|issue=5|pages=1659–1662|doi=10.1103/physrev.170.1659|bibcode=1968PhRv..170.1659S }}</ref> aka "Sugawara Construction" of the energy-momentum tensor.

==Early life==

Sugawara was born in 1938 as a son of a [[Zen Buddhist]] in [[Miyagi, Japan]].  He obtained his BSc in Physics (1961), MSc in Physics (1963), and PhD in Physics (1966), from the [[University of Tokyo]].<ref name="JSPSUSA Sugawara Profile">{{cite web|url=http://jspsusa.org/FORUM1997/bio.sugawara.html| title=JSPS Washington Office Sugawara Profile|website=Japan Society for the Promotion of Science Washington Office|access-date=September 8, 2014}}</ref>

==Academic career==
[[File:Hirotaka Sugawara cropped 1 Hirotaka Sugawara 20010702.jpg|thumb|left|200px|Sugawara attended the Snowmass Conference (July 2, 2001)]]
[[File:Hirotaka Sugawara cropped 1 Hirotaka Sugawara 20141210.jpg|thumb|left|200px|Sugawara established Advanced Medical Instrumentation Unit at [[Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology]]]]

When Sugawara was still a graduate student at the University of Tokyo, he derived a relation for non-leptonic hyperon decay amplitudes called "Lee-Sugawara relation" while studying the symmetry of weak interactions.<ref name="KEK News Vol 3 No 1">{{cite web|title=Hirotaka Sugawara Received the Medal with Purple Ribbon|url=http://legacy.kek.jp/kek-news/Vol3_No1/p10.html|website=High Energy Accelerator Research Organization (KEK)|access-date=September 8, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402114142/http://legacy.kek.jp/kek-news/Vol3_No1/p10.html|archive-date=April 2, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> He received his doctorate from the University of Tokyo in 1966, and has held postdoctoral research positions at Cornell University, [[University of California, Berkeley]], and [[University of Chicago]].  Upon his return to Japan in 1968, he became a research associate at Tokyo University of Education, and he joined the University of Tokyo as an assistant professor in 1971.<ref name="KEK News Vol 3 No 1" />  "A Field Theory of Currents"<ref name="field theory of currents" /> is known as the ""Sugawara model," a dynamical model of local currents, in which the energy momentum tensor was expressed as a product of currents,"<ref name="Gross 2004 Nobel Lecture">{{cite web|title=D. J. Gross's 2004 Nobel Lecture|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/2004/gross-lecture.html|website=Nobel Prize.org|access-date=September 8, 2014}}</ref> which opened the door to the algebraic formulation of field theories.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Sugawara|first1=Hirotaka|title=My 50 years of research in particle physics|journal=Proceedings of the Japan Academy, Series B|date=April 2010|volume=86|issue=4|pages=293–302|url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/pjab/86/4/86_4_293/_article|doi=10.2183/pjab.86.293|pmid=20431257|pmc=3417796|bibcode=2010PJAB...86..293S }}</ref>

In 1975, he was promoted to a full professor at the National Laboratory for High Energy Physics (today known as High Energy Accelerator Research Organization (KEK)), where he served as the Director General from 1989 to 2003.<ref name="KEK News Vol 3 No 1" /> While serving as the Director General at KEK, he concurrently held positions (professor, councilor, Dean, and steering committee member) at various organizations such as the Graduate University for Advanced Studies (SOKENDAI), National Institute for Physiological Science (NIPS), National Institute of Polar Research (NIPR), National Institute for Fusion Science (NIFS), Okazaki National Research Institutes, and Institutes of Space and Astronautical Science (ISAS).<ref name="KEK News Vol 3 No 1" /> He also served as a Chair of the International Committee for Future Accelerators (ICFA), a working group of the [[International Union of Pure and Applied Physics]], from 1999 to 2002.<ref name=IFCA>{{cite web|title=IFCA Membership|url=http://www.fnal.gov/directorate/icfa/membership.html|website=International Committee for Future Accelerators|access-date=September 8, 2014}}</ref> KEKB, also called a B-factory for its copious production of B-mesons, is a particle accelerator used in the Belle experiment to study CP violation.  He contributed significantly to the B-factory project as the Director General of KEK (the Japanese National Laboratory for High Energy Physics).<ref name="KEK News Vol 3 No 1" /> He also provided strong leadership in setting up the long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiment connecting the proton synchrotron at KEK (the High Energy Accelerator Research Organization) and [[Super-Kamiokande]] (Super-Kamioka Neutrino Detection Experiment, abbreviated to Super-K or SK) in Kamioka, Gifu.<ref name="OIST Sugawara Overview">{{cite web|title=Overview of Prof Sugawara's Achievements|url=http://www.oist.jp/sites/default/files/img/articles/20130513_sugawara-order-sacred-treasure/Prof.%20Sugawara%20Achievements.pdf|website=Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST)|access-date=September 8, 2014}}</ref> He led the launch of J-PARC (Japan Proton Accelerator Research Complex) that was jointly developed between KEK and JAEA (the [[Japan Atomic Energy Agency]]).<ref name="OIST Sugawara Overview" />

After serving as the Director General of KEK for 14 years, he became a Professor Emeritus at KEK and a professor at University of Hawaii, Manoa, in 2003.<ref name=Nishina>{{cite web|title=Nishina Memorial Foundation|url=http://www.nishina-mf.or.jp/NishinaMemorialPrize-E.html|website=Nishina Memorial Foundation|access-date=September 8, 2014}}</ref> Concurrently he also served on the Mombusho Council for Research, and for other science councils in Japan.<ref name=UHawaii>{{cite web|title=Colleges of Arts & Sciences to Host Public Lecture Featuring World Renowned Physicist Hirotaka Sugawara|url=http://www.hawaii.edu/news/article.php?aId=648|website=University of Hawai'i|access-date=September 8, 2014}}</ref> In 2004, he held an Executive Director position at Sokendai Graduate University for Advanced Studies.<ref name="OIST Grad Sch Sugawara Profile">{{cite web|title=Distinguished Professor Hirotaka Sugawara Profile|url=https://groups.oist.jp/grad/hirotaka-sugawara|website=OIST Graduate University|access-date=September 8, 2014}}</ref> He became a Director (Washington DC Office) of Japanese Society for the Promotion of Science (JSPS) in 2008.<ref name="JSPSUSA Sugawara Profile" /><ref name="KEK News Vol 3 No 1" />

Since 2012, he has been serving Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) as a Distinguished Professor and also as a Special Advisor to the President.<ref name="OIST Sugawara Overview" /><ref name="OIST Grad Sch Sugawara Profile" /><ref name="OIST News Innovative Academic">{{cite web|title=The Innovative Academic: OIST Welcomes Hirotaka Sugawara|url=http://www.oist.jp/eventreport/innovative-academic-oist-welcomes-hirotaka-sugawara|website=Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST)|date=April 17, 2012 |access-date=September 8, 2014}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
[[File:Hirotaka Sugawara cropped 2 Hirotaka Sugawara 20130513.jpg|thumb|200px|Sugawara wore the [[Order of the Sacred Treasure|Order of the Sacred Treasure, Gold Rays with Neck Ribbon]] around his neck. (May 13, 2013)]]

* 17th Nishina Memorial Prize, 1971<ref name=Nishina />
* 36th Toray Science and Technology Prize, 1996<ref name=Toray>{{cite web|title=List of winners 1990 (31st) – 1999 (40th) Toray Science and Technology Prize : List of Winners|url=http://www.toray.com/tsf/kagaku/kag_004.html|website=Toray|access-date=September 8, 2014|archive-date=October 13, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141013025235/http://www.toray.com/tsf/kagaku/kag_004.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* [[Medals of Honor (Japan)|Medal of Honor with Purple Ribbon]], Japan, 1999<ref name="KEK News Vol 3 No 1" />
* [[Order of the Sacred Treasure|Order of the Sacred Treasure, Gold Rays with Neck Ribbon]], 2013<ref name="OIST Sacred Treasure Article">{{cite web|title=Prof. Hirotaka Sugawara Receives the Order of the Sacred Treasure|url=http://www.oist.jp/news-center/news/2013/5/13/prof-hirotaka-sugawara-receives-order-sacred-treasure|website=Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST)|date=May 13, 2013 |access-date=September 8, 2014}}</ref>

==Selected publications==
* Hirotaka Sugawara, "Application of Current Commutation Rules to Nonleptonic Decay of Hyperons", [[Physical Review Letters]], Vol.15, Issue 22, [[American Physical Society]], November 29, 1965, pp.&nbsp;870–873. {{ISSN|0031-9007}}
* Hirotaka Sugawara, "A Field Theory of Currents", Physical Review, Vol.170, Issue 5, American Physical Society, June 25, 1968, pp.&nbsp;1659–1662. {{ISSN|0031-899X}}[3]
* Tohru Eguchi and Hirotaka Sugawara, "Extended model of elementary particles based on an analogy with superconductivity", Physical Review D, Vol.10, Issue 12, American Physical Society, December 15, 1974, pp.&nbsp;4257–4262. {{ISSN|1550-7998}}
* H. Sugawara, "Isobar production and the SU3 symmetry", Physics Letters, Vol.9, Issue 1, Elsevier, March 15, 1964, pp.&nbsp;60–62.
* Hirotaka Sugawara, "Application of Current Commutation Rules to Nonleptonic Decay of Hyperons", Physical Review Letters, Vol.15, Issue 25, American Physical Society, December 20, 1965, pp.&nbsp;870–873. {{ISSN|0031-9007}}
* Hirotaka Sugawara and Frank von Hippel, "Zero-Parameter Model of the N–N Potential", Physical Review, Vol.172, Issue 5, American Physical Society, August 25, 1968, pp.&nbsp;1764–1788. {{ISSN|0031-899X}}
* Hirotaka Sugawara, "Theory of Currents-How to Break the Symmetry", Physical Review Letters, Vol.21, Issue 11, American Physical Society, September 9, 1968, pp.&nbsp;772–775. {{ISSN|0031-9007}}
* Jiro Arafune and Hirotaka Sugawara, "Breakdown of the Pomeranchuk Theorem and the Behavior of the Leading J-Plane Singularity", Physical Review Letters, Vol.25, Issue 21, American Physical Society, November 23, 1970, pp.&nbsp;1516–1518. {{ISSN|0031-9007}}
* Hirotaka Sugawara, "Relativistic collective motion", Physical Review D, Vol.12, Issue 10, American Physical Society, November 15, 1975, pp.&nbsp;3272–3278. {{ISSN|1550-7998}}
* Sandip Pakvasa and Hirotaka Sugawara, "CP violation in the six-quark model", Physical Review D, Vol.14, Issue 1, American Physical Society, July 1, 1976, pp.&nbsp;305–308. {{ISSN|1550-7998}}
* Hirotaka Sugawara, "Theory of quark confinement based on an analogy with a theory of magnetic monopoles", Physical Review D, Vol.14, Issue 10, American Physical Society, November 15, 1976, pp.&nbsp;2764–2772. {{ISSN|1550-7998}}
* Sandip Pakvasa and Hirotaka Sugawara, "Evading the axion without massless quarks", Physical Review D, Vol.19, Issue 7, American Physical Society, April 1, 1979, pp.&nbsp;2225–2226. {{ISSN|1550-7998}}
* Hirotaka Sugawara, "Dynamical calculation of quark, lepton, and gauge-boson masses", Physical Review D, Vol.30, Issue 11, American Physical Society, December 1, 1984, pp.&nbsp;2396–2407. {{ISSN|1550-7998}}
* Hirotaka Sugawara, "String in curved space: Use of spinor representation of a noncompact group", Physical Review Letters, Vol.56, Issue 2, American Physical Society, January 13, 1986, pp.&nbsp;103–106. {{ISSN|0031-9007}}
